lesson.text: Quick memory: last unit, particles. What is all matter made of? Particles, too small to see, that are always moving.
Mass is the amount of matter in something. We measure it with scales, in grams and kilograms.
When matter changes, melts, dissolves or mixes, the total mass stays the same. No matter is made or lost.
Melt a 100 g ice cube in a closed bag and you get 100 g of water. The ice changed state, but no matter came in or went out.
Dissolve 10 g of salt in 200 g of water: the salty water has a mass of 210 g, even though you can't see the salt any more.
If a gas escapes, like fizz from a drink, the mass seems to drop because some matter left. In a sealed container, it stays the same.
Try it in the world: at a Science Lab bench, do "Melting and freezing": the ice becomes water and then ice again, the same matter every time. Next: the properties of materials.

exercises.prompt: When ice melts, its mass stays the same.
exercises.hint: Is any matter lost?
exercises.explain: Yes: the water has the same mass as the ice.

exercises.prompt: What do we use to measure mass?
exercises.hint: Think of weighing flour.
exercises.explain: Scales measure mass, in grams and kilograms.

exercises.prompt: A 50 g chocolate bar melts. What is the mass of the melted chocolate?
exercises.hint: Melting doesn't add or remove matter.
exercises.explain: It is still 50 g: melting keeps the mass.

exercises.prompt: When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar's mass disappears.
exercises.hint: Is the sugar still there?
exercises.explain: No: the sugar is still there, so its mass is still there too.

exercises.prompt: Which unit measures mass?
exercises.hint: Which unit would a kitchen scale show when you weigh flour?
exercises.explain: Mass is measured in grams and kilograms.

exercises.prompt: 20 g of salt is stirred into 300 g of water. What is the mass of the salty water?
exercises.hint: Add the two masses.
exercises.explain: 300 g + 20 g = 320 g. The salt's mass is still there.

exercises.prompt: A 200 g snowman melts in a sealed tub. What does the water weigh?
exercises.hint: Nothing got in or out.
exercises.explain: In a sealed tub, the mass stays at 200 g.

exercises.prompt: 150 g of sand is mixed with 50 g of pebbles. What is the total mass?
exercises.hint: Nothing is lost when you mix them. What do you do with the two masses?

exercises.prompt: Breaking a 30 g biscuit into crumbs leaves 30 g of crumbs.
exercises.hint: Did any biscuit go away?
exercises.explain: Yes: the crumbs still have all of the biscuit's mass.

exercises.prompt: Why does an open glass of fizzy drink lose a little mass over time?
exercises.hint: Where do the bubbles go?
choices: Gas bubbles escape into the air.
exercises.explain: The gas escapes into the air, taking its mass with it.

exercises.prompt: Vinegar and baking soda fizz inside a sealed bag. Before: 250 g. What is the mass after?
exercises.hint: The gas is trapped in the bag.
exercises.explain: The new gas stays in the sealed bag, so the mass stays at 250 g.

exercises.prompt: The same fizzing mix in an open cup gets lighter. Why?
exercises.hint: Is the cup sealed?
choices: The gas it makes escapes into the air.
exercises.explain: The gas leaves the open cup, so the scales show less.

exercises.prompt: A 500 g block of ice melts to water, then the water freezes again. What does it weigh now?
exercises.hint: Melting and freezing keep the mass.
exercises.explain: Still 500 g: no matter was added or lost.

exercises.prompt: If you dissolve 5 g of sugar in 100 g of water, you can get the sugar back by letting the water dry up.
exercises.hint: What is left when water dries up?
exercises.explain: Yes: 5 g of sugar crystals are left behind.

exercises.prompt: Order these from least to most mass.
exercises.hint: The salty water has both.
items: the salt dissolved in the water
exercises.explain: 20 g, then 200 g, then 220 g of salty water.

exercises.prompt: 30 g of sugar is stirred into 250 g of water. What is the mass of the sweet water, in grams?
exercises.hint: Dissolving keeps all the sugar's mass. Add the two masses.
exercises.explain: 250 + 30 = 280 g: the sugar is still there, only too spread out to see.

exercises.prompt: Sort the changes: does the total mass stay the same, or does some leave?
items: ice melts in a sealed bag
a drink fizzes in an open glass
exercises.hint: Ask: can any matter get out, like a gas escaping into the air?
exercises.explain: Melting in a sealed bag, dissolving and breaking keep all the matter. Fizz and steam escape into the air, taking their mass with them.

exercises.prompt: Match each change to what happens to its mass.
exercises.hint: Only one of them lets matter leave.
exercises.explain: Melting and dissolving keep every bit of matter, so the mass stays. Escaping gas takes matter away.

exercises.prompt: Sort the changes: melting, dissolving or mixing?
exercises.hint: Does a solid turn to a liquid, spread through a liquid, or just sit with other things?
exercises.explain: Melting: ice to water, butter in a warm pan. Dissolving: salt in water, sugar in tea. Mixing: sand and pebbles, nuts and raisins. In all of them, the total mass stays the same.

exercises.prompt: In a sealed bag, 40 g of baking soda and 160 g of vinegar fizz. Then the bag is opened and 5 g of gas escapes. What mass is left in the bag, in grams?
exercises.hint: Sealed, nothing leaves. Once it is open, take away what escaped.
exercises.explain: Sealed, the mass stays 40 + 160 = 200 g. Once opened, 5 g of gas escapes: 200 − 5 = 195 g. The matter left the bag; it was not destroyed.
